transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-05
Start time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Evan Rios (Redwood), Maya Singh (CTO, Cobalt), Luis Ortega (Head of ML), Hannah Park (Infra)

Summary:
Cobalt is evaluating Redwood's Dedicated offering for production inference. Primary drivers: isolation + data controls for regulated customers, predictable latency for SLAs, and burst capacity during nightly retrain/real-time scoring spikes. They currently run models on a mixed fleet (K8s on AWS + some Nvidia GPU RIs) and are exploring a reserved GPU pool with controlled fallbacks to hosted for overflow. Key asks: pricing clarity for reserved vs burst, isolation guarantees, VPC connectivity, SOC2/audit artifacts, and a plan to run benchmarks with their 13B LLM (quantized) at 8–12 qps baseline with nightly spikes to 60 qps.

Topics covered:
- Current infra and pain points
- Isolation and compliance requirements (data residency, audit logs)
- Burst/fallback strategy and cost tradeoffs
- Benchmark plan: 2-hour pilot with sample traces
- Config knobs: batching, KV cache, quantization, model pinning

Action items (auto): see action_items field above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samira (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Samira here from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. Can you hear me okay?
[00:06] Maya (Cobalt): Yep, loud and clear. Thanks.
[00:09] Samira: Awesome. Quick intros? We'll just do a quick round and then hand to Daniel for the infra questions.
[00:15] Luis (Cobalt): Luis Ortega, Head of ML. I'm responsible for model infra and serving at Cobalt.
[00:18] Hannah: Hannah Park, infra engineer, networking and security.
[00:20] Daniel (Redwood SE): Daniel Cho, solutions engineer, I get into the nitty gritty on runtime and capacity.
[00:24] Evan (Redwood): Evan Rios, solutions — I'll help with benchmarks and ops patterns.
[00:27] Samira: Great. High-level, you sent over a note that you're evaluating dedicated reserved GPUs for production. Can you walk us through the goals and constraints?
[00:36] Maya: Yeah. So we're moving to production for our real-time scoring product. It's latency-sensitive — p95 under 220ms is kind of our goal for user-facing RT endpoints. We also have enterprise customers that need strict data isolation and audit logs. Today we run on AWS EKS with some reserved GPU instances but performance is all over the place during peak hours. The peaks are predictable — evenings and batch re-score at 2am.
[01:00] Luis: To add, our models are a mix — mostly a quantized 13B LLM for conversation/assist and smaller rerankers. Typical baseline is 8–12 qps but we want headroom to 50–70 qps during batch windows. We don't want cold starts or heavy latency variability.
[01:18] Daniel: Okay good. Do you have multi-tenant concerns where different business units run on the same cluster?
[01:22] Maya: Yes. Right now it's shared, which is the problem. Some teams run long-running batches and noisy neighbors impact latency. So isolation is a big requirement. We're exploring Redwood Dedicated for a reserved pool per environment and possibly per BU.
[01:36] Samira: Understood. On the isolation side we provide dedicated GPU pools with tenancy guarantees, VPC peering options, and private control plane for Private deployments. For Dedicated: customers can get logical isolation and network-level restrictions. Hannah, any specific network or encryption needs?
[01:51] Hannah: We need SAML SSO for console, KMS integration for key management, and we require outbound IP ranges for allowlisting. Also audit logs stored 1 year minimum. SOC2 or equivalent docs are a must.
[02:05] Samira: Yep, we'll share the security pack with SOC2, ISO, and the network diagram. KMS integrations supported; for Dedicated we can integrate your KMS or use customer-managed keys depending on the plan.
[02:15] Luis: How do you handle burst? We want reserved GPUs for baseline and then burst to either Redwood Hosted or an overprovisioned pool. What's typical?
[02:24] Daniel: Two patterns we see: 1) reserved baseline pool sized for steady qps and set autoscaling policies with burst capacity as a paid add-on (burst buffer), and 2) policy-based routing that sends overflow to the hosted tier or to a lower-capacity quantized variant. Both have tradeoffs — the hosted fallback gives elastic capacity but you lose some isolation guarantees and may have slight variance in model version.
[02:47] Evan: For cost predictability, some customers keep a small burst buffer reserved (e.g., 20% extra GPUs) and route rare high spikes to hosted. That keeps SLA and isolation for normal traffic and limits egress to hosted only during true spikes.
[02:59] Maya: Could you do model pinning so the hosted fallback always uses the same model hash? We need deterministic outputs.
[03:06] Daniel: Yes, we support model pinning and model variant alignment. We can pin an exact artifact and deploy compatible quantized variants in hosted to reduce drift. There is an ops tradeoff but it's doable.
[03:18] Luis: On the runtime side, what's the latencies we should expect for a quantized 13B on your hardware? Ballpark p95 and p99?
[03:27] Daniel: Ballpark on latest A100/RTX variants: single-token step latencies vary, but in practice with continuous batching and KV caching we see p95s down around 80–160ms depending on sequence length. For end-to-end generation with typical 40 tokens it can sit around the 150–250ms p95. We will run your exact model in our pilot to give Cobalt numbers.
[03:50] Hannah: And during those spikes, do you pre-warm KV caches or re-use sessions? Our batch jobs are heavy on context reuse.
[03:57] Evan: Yes, we support prefix/KV caching and session affinity to keep cache warm. That significantly lowers tail latency for repeated contexts. We'll ask for traces so we can simulate cache hit ratios in the benchmark.
[04:09] Maya: Any constraints around quantization formats? We're using 4-bit Q8-like approach.
[04:14] Daniel: We support multiple quant formats; our runtime has quantization-friendly execution paths. We'll recommend a config but we usually benchmark both 4-bit and 8-bit to see perf/quality tradeoffs.
[04:24] Samira: Can you talk budget? What's the rough monthly commit you're thinking about?
[04:28] Maya: We want to start small — maybe a 6-month pilot with 6 reserved GPUs and see how it scales. If that meets SLAs we could convert to a 12–24 month commit for production. What does 6 GPUs translate to in throughput for 13B?
[04:40] Daniel: Depends on batching and concurrency. Rough rule: with smart batching and 1–2 concurrent streams per GPU you can get up to X qps (we avoided hard numbers), but we'll give precise numbers after we run your workload in the pilot. For planning, it would likely cover your baseline if you tune batching. We'll provide sizing guidance.
[04:58] Luis: We also need a canary/rollout plan. We can't risk a model rollback that affects customers.
[05:03] Evan: Our Console supports per-route model pinning, canary percentage rollouts, and automatic fallback. You can route a small percentage to a new variant and monitor quality regressions through Redwood Optimize.
[05:14] Hannah: On private deployments: If we go private (VPC/on-prem), what changes? Network latency? Control plane?
[05:21] Daniel: Private gives you a customer-managed control plane and optional on-prem runtime. Network is local to your VPC, so latency can improve, but operational overhead and minimum commitments are higher. For most, Dedicated with VPC peering covers the isolation requirement without going fully private.
[05:37] Maya: How does billing work for burst? Is it per-token billed on hosted fallback and flat for reserved?
[05:43] Samira: Reserved is monthly commit (capacity units) and you still get per-token metrics for cost visibility. Bursts to hosted are billed per-token on top of the reserved fee. We can model scenarios in the pricing spreadsheet.
[05:56] Luis: Any logs retention and export features? We need to ship audit logs to Splunk and keep model inference logs for 1 year.
[06:03] Daniel: You can configure log sinks (S3, GCS) and we support forwarding to SIEMs. Audit logs retention is configurable; for Dedicated we support 1 year out-of-the-box and longer on request.
[06:15] Maya: Okay. Can we outline the pilot? We're keen to run a short benchmark with our quantized 13B and production traces.
[06:22] Evan: Recommended: 2-hour scheduled benchmark where we run synthetic and replayed traces. We'll size reserved pool for baseline, then ramp to spikes. We'll capture p50/p95/p99, token cost, and memory profiles. We'll also test KV cache hit scenarios.
[06:36] Hannah: We'll need network playbook — VPN or VPC? Which is fastest to set up?
[06:40] Samira: VPC peering or PrivateLink are common. For a quick pilot VPN is sometimes faster but VPC peering is more robust. We'll send a networking checklist.
[06:50] (short cross talk)
[07:00] Maya: About SLAs — what uptime SLA do you offer for Dedicated?
[07:03] Samira: We offer SLA-backed uptime and latency targets for Dedicated; the exact numbers depend on the commitment level. We'll surface those in the contract and pricing doc.
[07:12] Luis: Any customers in our vertical? We do a lot of regulated finance analytics.
[07:16] Samira: Yes, we have a few finance and healthcare customers on Dedicated and Private. We'll share anonymized case studies.
[07:22] Daniel: Quick technical note on fallbacks — if you route to hosted, you can set a model variant that is quant-equivalent to minimize drift. Also request-level routing can prefer ded-pools first, then fallback based on queue depth or latency SLO breach.
[07:37] Hannah: Is there an option for resident GPUs per BU? We might want separate pools to enforce billing and quotas.
[07:43] Evan: You can create multiple reserved pools and split by BU; it's a bit of a contract/ops setup but fully supported.
[07:51] Maya: On telemetry, we need token-level cost reporting mapped to customer accounts. Does Redwood console provide that?
[07:58] Samira: Yes, the Console provides token-level cost breakdowns and you can tag routes to map back to customer billing.
[08:05] Luis: One more — model update velocity. We retrain weekly; what's the recommended rollout cadence to avoid frequent rollbacks?
[08:11] Daniel: Weekly is common; use canary rollouts with automated quality checks (we can plug Redwood Optimize/eval harness). If you see regressions, automatic rollback policies can revert to the previous pinned artifact.
[08:24] (brief pause)
[08:28] Maya: This is helpful. I'd like to see a concrete cost example for our 6 GPU pilot plus a 20% burst buffer and what overflow to hosted looks like for 1% of the time.
[08:38] Samira: We'll build that and include token cost assumptions, burst costs, and a conversion to monthly spend.
[08:43] Hannah: We'll also need the security pack and an initial network diagram.
[08:46] Samira: Yep, will send.
[08:48] Evan: For the benchmark, if you can send sample traces and model weights (or a dockerized artifact), we'll prepare a test plan and get back with a recommended pool size.
[08:57] Luis: We'll send traces and a small artifact. For regulatory reasons we may scrub PII.
[09:02] Samira: Totally fine. We'll support synthetic replays.
[09:05] (wrap up)
[09:07] Samira: To recap: Redwood will send pricing, SOC2/security pack, networking checklist; SEs will prepare config and benchmarking plan; Cobalt will share traces and model artifacts; schedule pilot week of 3/16.
[09:20] Maya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:22] Samira: Thanks — we'll follow up in email and drop the docs.
[09:25] (meeting ends)
